p.challenge: Four equal +1 μC charges sit at the corners of a square. By superposition the net field is the vector sum of four kq/r² fields. Find the point where they cancel (E = 0) and explain why it must be there.
A single +2 μC charge: E = kQ/r², pointing radially outward. Move the probe P to a point where E = 2 × 10⁷ N/C. How far from the charge is it? Is every such point on a circle?
Like charges +4 μC and +1 μC are 9 cm apart. Find the neutral point where E = 0. Is it nearer the smaller charge? Check with k(4)/r₁² = k(1)/r₂², so r₁ = 2r₂.

A dipole: ±1 μC, 2 cm apart (p = 2 × 10⁻⁸ C m, pointing up). On its axis 10 cm away, E ≈ 2kp/r³ = 3.6 × 10⁵ N/C. Find the point on the equatorial line (the x-axis here) where E is half that, 1.8 × 10⁵ N/C. Which way does E point there?
A dipole of p = 4 × 10⁻⁹ C m (±200 nC, 2 cm apart) sits in a uniform field of 5 × 10⁴ N/C. Turn it until the torque τ = pE sin θ is 1 × 10⁻⁴ N m. Notice the net force stays zero.
Gauss's law: Φ = q_enc/ε₀, whatever the shape of the surface. Draw a closed surface whose net flux is (4 μC)/ε₀ ≈ 4.5 × 10⁵ N m² C⁻¹. Can you find two different ways?
Draw a closed surface that has charges inside it but ZERO net flux. Charges outside send in as many lines as out, so only q_enc matters.
A charge of 6 × 10⁻⁷ C (0.6 μC): V = kQ/r falls off as 1/r. Find a point where V = 4.5 × 10⁴ V. How far is it? How much work brings a 3 nC charge there from infinity (W = qV)?
+3 μC and −1 μC: potentials add as scalars, V = k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂). Find a point where V = 0. It lies nearer the smaller charge — and is E zero there too?
U = −pE cos θ. Turn the dipole (p = 2 μC × 4 cm = 8 × 10⁻⁸ C m, E = 10⁵ N/C) to its stable equilibrium, where U is minimum. How much work would it take to turn it from there to 180°? (W = 2pE)
Ohm's law: V = IR. Each battery block here gives 6 V. Get a current of exactly 0.4 A — 12 V across 30 Ω is one way; find another. Does V/I change for the same resistor?
Inside a solenoid B = µ₀nI, so the field depends on turns × current. With the core in, pick up exactly 6 paperclips (1200 ampere-turns). Find two different ways to do it.
The pole labels are hidden. Outside a magnet, field lines run from N to S and a compass needle lines up along them. Use the compasses to find the N pole, then show the iron-filing pattern.
Soft iron is a ferromagnet: its domains line up with the coil’s field and make the magnet far stronger. Lift at least 8 paperclips, then take out the iron core and watch what happens.

p.title: Does the galvanometer deflect?

items.text: Bar magnet pushed into the coil
Bar magnet held still inside the coil
items.why: No change in flux, no emf

items.text: Bar magnet pulled out of the coil
items.why: Flux decreases — deflection the other way

items.text: Coil moved towards a stationary magnet
Magnet and coil moved together at the same velocity
items.why: No relative motion, so the flux does not change

items.text: Switch of the nearby primary coil is closed
items.why: Current rises, so its flux through the second coil changes (brief deflection)

items.text: Steady current flows in the primary coil
items.why: Steady current → steady flux → no induced emf

items.text: Switch of the primary coil is opened
items.why: Current falls to zero: brief deflection the opposite way

items.text: Current-carrying coil moved towards the second coil
items.why: Flux linked with the second coil increases

p.challenge: Faraday and Henry's experiments: decide in which cases a current is induced.

Series LCR: R = 30 Ω, X_L = 80 Ω, X_C = 40 Ω, I = 2 A (RMS). V_R = IR = 60 V is in phase with I; V_X = V_L − V_C = I(X_L − X_C) leads I by 90°. Drag the V_X phasor into place (1 grid unit = 10 V) and read the resultant (the supply voltage) and φ. What is Z = V/I?
Series LCR: L = 0.5 H, C = 8 µF, R = 10 Ω on a 10 V (RMS) supply, I = V/√(R² + (ωL − 1/ωC)²). Drag along the resonance curve to the peak. Check ω₀ = 1/√(LC) and I = V/R there.

p.challenge: Place each radiation in the right part of the spectrum.

Concave mirror with f = 20 cm (f = −20 cm in the Cartesian convention). Place the object so the image forms 60 cm from the mirror. There are two places — find both and check 1/v + 1/u = 1/f and m = −v/u.
Concave mirror, f = 15 cm: find where the image is real, inverted and the same size as the object. Then switch to the convex mirror: can it ever give a real image?
Snell's law: sin i / sin r = n₂₁. Make the ray bend to r = 30° inside water (n = 1.33), then inside crown glass. Why can't diamond reach r = 30°?
Convex lens, f = +20 cm. Place the object so a REAL image forms 60 cm from the lens and read m = v/u. Then try the concave lens: can |v| ever reach 60 cm?
A simple magnifier: convex lens, f = 6.25 cm. Move the ant inside the focal length so its virtual image forms at the near point, 25 cm from the lens. Then m = 1 + D/f = 5.

x-axis: frequency ν (in 10¹⁴ Hz); y-axis: stopping potential V₀ (V). V₀ = 0 at ν = 5 and V₀ = 2 V at ν = 10. Make the line pass through both points. Its slope is h/e; where it cuts the ν-axis is the threshold ν₀.
